newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France accused of organising Zaire succession.
newsitem.headline: France accused of organising Zaire succession.

text.p: France wanted ailing Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko to go back to Zaire to sort out a successor who is friendly to French interests, a leading Belgian expert on Zaire said on Friday.

"France does not want Mobutu to die on French soil, it wants him to go back and organise his succession," said Colette Braeckman, a journalist for Le Soir newspaper and author of several books on Zaire.

Earlier today, Mobutu left France for Zaire where large parts of the eastern territories are occupied by rebels led by Laurent Kabila. Mobutu was recovering from cancer treatment in his villa in southern France.
Braeckman blasted France for playing what she called a "neo-colonialist role" in Africa.

"The French role in the Great Lakes region is catastrophic. It is part of French mythology to believe that these are French-speaking countries, and that therefore France has the right to play Viceroy there," she said in a speech at the Columbia University Club of Belgium.
She said Belgium was much better placed to play a role in post-Mobutu Zaire, because it cut ties with him in the early nineties.
"Belgium, like the U.S., supports the pan-African view that it is better to let Africans sort out their own problems," she said.
She said that Kabila, if he reaches his goal of overthrowing Mobutu's regime, would be more likely to open relationships with other countries than France.
She also said that she did not believe there would be a war over the succession or the country would fall apart if Mobutu dies or is overthrown.
"Maybe Mobutu's only accomplishment is that he has built a national feeling," said Braeckman, who in 1992 was refused entry to Zaire for criticising Mobutu in one of her books.

Braeckman said that between Kabila and Etienne Tshisekedi -- leader of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), Zaire's main opposition group -- there was a broad understanding about the need for elections.
"Tshisekedi is a hugely popular, old-fashioned, non-violent democrat. One solution (for a post-Mobutu Zaire) could be in the sharing of power between him and Kabila," she said.
It would be wise to have a two-year transition period before organising elections, she added. "If you hold elections now, Kabila would get 90 percent of the votes, of course."
Braeckman said she did not expect Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, former head of the transitional parliament, to play a major role in the manoevring over the succession to Mobutu.
She said he is hated in Zaire for having helped prime minister Kengo Wa Dondo get his job.
Kengo has been under fire for months for failing to stem the rebels' advance in the east.
